result.summary: After Jupiter calms the gods by saying even he is bound by the Fates, Miletus flees Crete and founds a city in Asia. His children Byblis and Caunus are born there. Byblis falls in love with her brother, writes to him, is rejected, pursues him as he flees, and dissolves into a fountain.

scenes.title: Jupiter calms the gods
scenes.summary: Jupiter tells the quarrelling gods that the Fates rule even him. He points to the aged Minos, who fears the young Miletus; Miletus flees to Asia and founds a city.
scenes.stakes: Minos fears losing his kingdom to Miletus; the gods' quarrel over the Fates is in play.

scenes.title: Byblis's love grows
scenes.summary: Cyane bears twins, Byblis and Caunus. Byblis's affection for her brother turns to desire and she dreams of embracing him.
scenes.stakes: Byblis risks her honour and peace of mind through forbidden desire.

scenes.title: Byblis debates with herself
scenes.summary: Waking, Byblis laments her dream and weighs the examples of the gods and Æolus's sons. She resolves to confess by letter.
scenes.stakes: Her honour and her brother's regard are at risk if she confesses.

scenes.title: The letter and rejection
scenes.summary: Byblis writes a confession and sends it by a servant; the tablets fall as an omen. Caunus reads part, rages and sends the servant away.
scenes.stakes: Byblis risks shame and rejection; the servant risks Caunus's violence.

scenes.title: Byblis resolves to persist
scenes.summary: Byblis blames her own haste and decides to try again. She keeps pressing Caunus until he flees his country and founds a new city.
scenes.stakes: She risks complete disgrace and loss of her brother.

scenes.title: Byblis becomes a fountain
scenes.summary: Mad with grief, Byblis wanders through Caria and Lycia after Caunus. She collapses, the Nymphs cannot console her, and she dissolves into a spring.
scenes.stakes: Byblis loses her sanity and finally her human form.

alias_notes.explanation: Byblis is also called a descendant of Apollo; Phœbus is a name of Apollo.
Bacchus is addressed by his mother's name.
Caunus is named after his grandfather, the river Mæander.

notable_quotes.reason: Jupiter admits that even he is subject to the Fates.
Ovid's moral about Byblis's forbidden love.
Byblis argues that passion suits youth, not laws.

analysis.text: Byblis's story studies obsession and self-deception: she rationalises her desire step by step, ignoring omens. It fits the book's recurring tales of forbidden love ending in transformation.
Her appeal to divine marriages of siblings reflects Roman debate about myth versus human law. The letter scene is an early psychological portrait of writing as persuasion.

legacy.text: Byblis's letter and monologue influenced later writers' treatment of incestuous or forbidden love, and the fountain's name reflects ancient aetiological tales about Caria.

fun_facts.text: The wax tablet and iron stylus Byblis uses were the ordinary Roman writing tools; erasing meant smoothing the wax.

language_notes.text: Iolaüs, Hercules' nephew and companion, was granted renewed youth for a day. The sons of Calirrhoë were likewise made grown men by prayer, in a divine intervention just before this scene.
Æacus, Rhadamanthus and Minos are Jupiter's sons, all famed as just men; the latter two were later judges of the dead.
Miletus is Phœbus (Apollo)'s son, so Minos fears a young, divinely fathered rival who could seize the throne.
The Mæander was a winding Asian river; 'returns to the same place' alludes to its looping course, which gave English the word 'meander'.
'Being known by thee' is a euphemism: Cyane has been sexually known by Miletus, who is the father of the twins.
'Sweetheart' renders a term of endearment; the translator's footnote notes the Latin 'domina' (mistress), a lover's word rather than a sister's.
Byblis invokes Venus and Cupid, gods of love, and Cupid's 'voluptuous mother' is Venus herself, so the address doubles up on the same goddess.
'By changing my name' means becoming his wife instead of his sister, so that she could be daughter-in-law to her own father.
Saturn, Ocean and Jove were Titans or gods who married their sisters (Ops, Tethys, Juno). Byblis cites them as precedent for sibling marriage.
Æolus, ruler of the winds, reportedly married his sons to his daughters. The best known pair is Macareus and Canace.
'Latent flame' means hidden love; the metaphor of fire for passion runs through the speech.
The iron pen is a stylus: a pointed rod used to scratch letters into the wax coating of a writing tablet.
She means she cannot plead her cause without naming herself, yet wishes to stay unidentified until her hopes of success are certain.
Cupid's 'ruthless weapon' is his arrow, which in myth inflicts the wound of love.
The 'example of the great Gods' refers to myths of divine incest, such as Jove (Zeus) marrying his sister Juno.
The wax tablets are too small for her words, so she squeezes the last line into the margin of the frame.
A 'pander' is a go-between who arranges illicit love affairs.
'Mæandrian' refers to the river Mæander in Asia Minor, the homeland of Caunus and Byblis.
Nautical metaphor: Byblis says she should have tested the wind with a little sail instead of spreading full canvas, as she now has.
Refers to the wax writing tablets she dropped when giving them to her servant, an omen she ignored before sending the letter.
Tigresses, lionesses, flint and adamant were conventional images for cruelty and hardness; she insists Caunus is not so pitiless.
Addressed to Bacchus (son of Semele). His women worshippers carried the thyrsus, a fennel staff topped with a pine cone, and celebrated his festival every third year.
The Chimæra was a fire-breathing monster of Lycia, part lion, goat and serpent; here it marks the mountain Byblis passes.
Favonius is the west wind, a gentle spring wind in Roman poetry.

context_notes.text: The gods have been quarrelling over whether to grant youth to mortals. Jupiter, king of the gods, steps in to end the dispute.
Minos was the powerful king of Crete, once feared across the sea for his naval strength.
Miletus was said to have founded the city of Miletus on the coast of Asia Minor (modern Turkey).
Caunus is Byblis's twin brother, son of Miletus and Cyanee. Byblis is in love with him.
Byblis recognises that the gods' customs are no guide for mortals, but her reasoning keeps drifting back toward self-justification.
Letters were sealed by pressing a signet ring into wax. Byblis uses tears for moisture because her mouth is dry, as one would normally wet the seal with the tongue.
Byblis is the twin sister of Caunus. Her hesitation before saying 'brother' shows how reluctant she is to admit the relationship she is violating.
Byblis has written a love letter to her twin brother Caunus, who has angrily rejected it.
Caunus's flight leads him to found a city, traditionally called Caunus, in Caria.
Bubasus was a place in Caria, so the Bubasian matrons are local Carian women.
Byblis descends from Phœbus (Apollo) through her grandfather. The spring called Byblis is the myth's explanation for a local fountain.

literary_notes.text: Repeating 'by the Fates' stresses that destiny, not ambition or force, governs life and aging.
Jupiter, the supreme god, admits he is powerless over the Fates, and cannot even spare his own sons from old age.
The narrator suddenly addresses Miletus directly, giving his flight a vivid, personal tone.
The narrator announces Byblis as a cautionary example, signalling her tragic end before the story unfolds.
The reader sees her desire for what it is while Byblis herself mistakes it for sisterly affection.
Her blush in sleep shows buried guilt and awareness she cannot admit while awake.
Delight is described as dissolving her marrow, a physical image that conveys how overwhelming the dream's pleasure was.
A run of questions shows her mind doubting itself, as she tries to dismiss the dream and cannot.
She addresses her desires as 'lawless flames' and orders them away, yet the command is undercut by her next thought.
Byblis half sees that she is kindling her own ruin, though she will not stop. The reader knows how her story ends.
The repeated 'and then' and the balanced paired verbs mimic Byblis's constant wavering and give the sentence a restless, vacillating rhythm.
Setting 'save' against 'destroy' frames her plea as a stark choice and shows her emotional manipulation of Caunus.
The falling tablets are a bad omen, hinting that her plea will fail.
Caunus fears disgrace to his own character, and his furious reaction is the opposite of the welcome Byblis hoped for.
The narrator addresses Byblis directly, heightening pity for her.
Her passion is a sea voyage, with sails and winds standing for her declaration of love and its risk.
Comparing Byblis to frenzied Bacchanals conveys her wild, uncontrolled grief as she runs howling across the fields.
The narrator's aside implies that tears forever flowing are the only gift the Naiads could give her, a bitter pity.
Piled-up comparisons of resin, bitumen and melting ice make her transformation slow, gentle and inevitable.
